To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
two isoforms of NT1 receptors exist and that one of them is expressed only early in development.

the NT1 neurotension receptor is differentially expressed in the developing rat cerebral cortex and hippocampus, and that the two isoforms of the receptor that have different glycosylation patterns are differentially expressed during development.

the NT1 receptor, like other G‐protein‐ coupled receptors, is expressed during development in two different isoforms: a short, immature isoform that is expressed transiently and a longer, mature isoform that is present throughout adulthood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and function of the central nervous system.
the neurobiological effects of neurotensin and its receptors.
understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the development of brain function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NT1 receptor is a G protein‐coupled receptor, which is expressed in many brain areas and in a variety of peripheral tissues.
the NT1 receptor is present at high levels in developing brain, and that this expression may be due to the presence of a novel, immature form of the protein.
the NT1 receptor is expressed at a higher level at birth and in the first 2 postnatal weeks than in the adult.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NT1 receptor is a G‐protein‐linked receptor that is widely distributed throughout the brain and that is developmentally regulated.
we have shown that the NT1 receptor is developmentally regulated in the rat brain and that there are two isoforms of the receptor, one of which is transiently expressed during early postnatal life.

the NT1 neurotension receptor is present in the rat brain from birth and that the 52kDa protein is a transitorily expressed, incompletely glycysylated form of the receptor that is mainly localized in the cytoplasm.

antibodies directed at different sequences of G protein‐coupled receptors can yield different labeling patterns in brain.
